**Base rate.** UKMTO’s November 20 review logged 148 vessel-damage reports across 263 days of conflict in the Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman. A simple Poisson conversion gives a 43% chance of at least one reportable event on a given day. That’s a rough baseline, not a count of qualifying days: multiple strikes can occur on the same day, and some qualifying incidents cause no damage. ([ukmto.org](https://www.ukmto.org/-/media/ukmto/products/20261120-ukmto_vra_overview_u.pdf?rev=5dbbfece42834c3896b685bc2223e1aa))

**What moves the estimate.** **Up:** JMIC’s November 22 update counted seven tanker strikes in Hormuz since November 16, including three on November 20–21. U.S.-assisted transits also rose from about 27 to 38 per day in the latest reporting period, so vessels continued to pass through despite the attacks. **Down:** Three of those strikes occurred within about 15 hours, so the strike count overstates how consistently attacks happen day to day. The November 22 UKMTO advisory about a tanker and military forces does not itself describe a qualifying act, so I don’t count it as evidence of another attack day. On balance, I put more weight on the recent surge than on the full-conflict average. ([ukmto.org](https://www.ukmto.org/-/media/ukmto/products/jmic_advisory_update_116_22-nov.pdf?rev=7d2a81d10d1d467cbe75f405f2392f59))

runs.reason:
The ongoing US-Israel-Iran conflict that began in late February 2026 has produced a sustained pattern of Iranian projectile strikes on merchant vessels, overwhelmingly outbound tankers, in the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent waters that fall inside the claim’s geographic scope. UKMTO’s own logs and contemporaneous JMIC updates show roughly one reported attack per day on average through 21 November (about 21 attack-classified reports in that span), with multiples on some days and occasional gaps; the implied daily probability of at least one qualifying report is therefore in the 0.65–0.75 range. JMIC continues to rate the Hormuz threat “severe” (attack highly likely), US-facilitated transits persist at roughly 25–30 vessels per day, and the most recent cluster (projectiles striking tankers 8–17 nm from Khasab on 20 and 21 November) shows the pattern has not broken.

Dated developments reinforce rather than reverse that base rate: attacks remain concentrated on the southern/outbound corridor that UKMTO and JMIC routinely publicize, oil-price and diplomatic pressure have not produced a pause, and time-late reports are explicitly accepted by the resolution rule. The principal uncertainty is ordinary day-to-day variance plus the possibility of a short operational lull.
